nameStory: This plant gave us the original marshmallow candy! For centuries, people extracted a sweet, gummy substance from the roots of marsh mallow plants to make confections and soothing throat lozenges. Today's puffy white marshmallows are made with gelatin instead, but they still carry the name of this humble wetland plant.
description: Marsh mallow is a soft, fuzzy perennial herb that grows 2-4 feet tall in wet places. The entire plant has a velvety, grayish-green appearance due to dense, soft hairs covering the stems and leaves. In late summer, it produces delicate pale pink or white flowers that look like small hollyhocks. Though native to Europe and Asia, it occasionally appears in New England as an escaped garden plant or naturalized specimen.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to oval leaves with soft, velvety texture that feels like flannel when you rub them between your fingers. The leaves are grayish-green and covered in dense, downy hairs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five-petaled flowers about 1 inch across, pale pink to white, clustered in the leaf joints. The petals have a papery texture and the flowers have the classic hibiscus-family look with prominent stamens.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, unbranched or little-branched stems that feel sturdy but soft due to the covering of fine hairs. The whole plant has a downy, almost silvery appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, flat seed pods that split into segments like a wheel of cheese. Each segment contains one kidney-shaped seed and feels papery when dry.

habitat: Look for marsh mallow in wet, marshy areas, along stream banks, and in coastal salt marshes. In New England, it's quite rare and usually found near the coast or in disturbed wetlands where it has escaped from cultivation. It prefers full sun and consistently moist to wet soils.

seasonality.spring: Young shoots emerge as fuzzy, grayish rosettes of heart-shaped leaves. The distinctive velvety texture is already apparent on new growth.
seasonality.summer: Stems reach full height and pale pink or white flowers begin appearing in July and August. This is the best time for identification when both the fuzzy leaves and hibiscus-like flowers are visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and distinctive wheel-like seed pods develop and split open. Leaves may turn yellowish but retain their soft, fuzzy texture until frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only dried stems and scattered seed pods. Not identifiable during this season.

funFact: The roots of marsh mallow contain up to 35% mucilage - a slimy, gel-like substance that becomes incredibly slippery when wet, which is why the phrase 'slippery as a marsh mallow root' was once common before we started saying 'slippery as an eel!'
confusionNotes: The velvety, grayish leaves make marsh mallow fairly distinctive, but it might be confused with other members of the mallow family. Remember: if it feels like soft flannel and grows in wet places, it's likely marsh mallow. Most other mallows prefer drier soils and have greener, less fuzzy leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Don't expect to find this plant easily - with only 3 recorded observations in New England, it's extremely rare here. Most 'marshmallow plants' you see in gardens are actually different species like rose mallow or swamp mallow, which are much more common and showy.
compareHints: Since marsh mallow is the only Althaea species commonly found in New England, compare it to other mallow family members like common mallow or rose mallow. Marsh mallow is distinguished by its consistently wet habitat, grayish-fuzzy appearance, and smaller, more delicate flowers compared to the large, showy blooms of rose mallow.
